name: The Pauline admission of gentiles
plain_explanation: Paul's decision to let non-Jews become Christians without first becoming Jews (i.e., without circumcision or following all of Jewish ceremonial law) is what allowed Christianity to grow beyond a small Jewish sect into a religion open to everyone in the Roman world.
precise_definition: The Pauline policy, contested by James and Peter, of admitting gentile converts to the Christian community without requiring circumcision or submission to the Mosaic Law, retaining Judaism's attractive features (moral certainty, sacred history) while removing the obstacles (circumcision, dietary law) that had limited its spread among gentiles.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as the single decision that made a universal religion out of what could otherwise have remained a reformed Judaism.
historical_origin: The controversy is recorded, from a Pauline point of view, in the Acts of the Apostles.
examples: Communities Paul founded composed of both Jewish and gentile converts
objections: James and (to a lesser extent) Peter wished Christianity to remain a reformed Judaism requiring full observance of the Law
competing_positions: The Jewish-Christian position of James and Peter
influence_on_later_thinkers: Set the template for Christianity as a universal rather than ethnic religion, in contrast to Judaism's continuing particularism.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly enabled Christianity's later political success as a mass religion capable of embracing the whole Roman population.
